hints: Focus on the physical states, homogeneous means catalyst and reactants are in the same phase, heterogeneous means they are in different phases.
In reaction 1 the reactants are all gases but the iron catalyst is a solid powder, so think about what that phase difference means.
In reaction 2 both the ozone reactants and the vaporised catalyst are in the gas phase, so link same phase to the catalyst type to finish the comparison.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definitions**

Think of it simply. Same phase means homogeneous, different phase means heterogeneous.

Rule to use:
$$\text{homogeneous: catalyst (phase) = reactants (phase)}$$ $$\text{heterogeneous: catalyst (phase) } \neq \text{ reactants (phase)}$$

**Classify reaction 1**

All reactants are gases, $\text{N}_2(g)$ and $\text{H}_2(g)$, but iron is a solid. Solid with gases means different phases.

Summary:
$$\text{Fe(s) + gases} \rightarrow \text{heterogeneous catalyst}$$

**Classify reaction 2**

Both ozone, $\text{O}_3(g)$, and the vaporised tetrachloromethane are gases. Gas with gas means the same phase.

Summary:
$$\text{vapour(g) + gases} \rightarrow \text{homogeneous catalyst}$$

**Combine to answer**

Reaction 1 is heterogeneous and reaction 2 is homogeneous. That matches only one statement, so you can confidently select it.

options.A: Incorrect. Reaction 1 is indeed heterogeneous (solid Fe with gaseous reactants), but reaction 2 is not. The vaporised catalyst is a gas mixing with gaseous ozone, so it cannot be heterogeneous.
options.B: Incorrect. Reaction 2 is indeed homogeneous (gas catalyst with gas reactants), but reaction 1 is not. Solid iron with gaseous reactants is the classic example of a heterogeneous catalyst in the Haber process.
options.C: Correct. Reaction 1 has $\text{Fe(s)}$ with $\text{N}_2(g)$ and $\text{H}_2(g)$, different phases so heterogeneous. Reaction 2 has vaporised (gaseous) catalyst with $\text{O}_3(g)$, same phase so homogeneous.
options.D: Incorrect. This reverses the truth. Students choosing this have swapped the definitions. Remember, solid catalyst in gas reaction is heterogeneous, not homogeneous.
